title: The Retail Sector in New York City
text:
## The Retail Sector in

## New York City

### Post-Pandemic Trends

September 2026 | Report 12-2027 
Prepared by the Office of the State Deputy Comptroller for the City of New York 
Deputy Comptroller Rahul Jain 

#### Introduction

The retail sector in New York City continues to undergo an uneven recovery since its downturn during the COVID-19 pandemic. While consumer spending rebounded quickly, driven in part by the expansion of e-commerce, its momentum has slowed, and inflation-adjusted retail taxable sales remain below pre-pandemic levels. Retail’s recovery has also lagged other major sectors as spending growth has shifted toward services, tourism has not fully rebounded, and commercial corridors continue to feel the effects of hybrid work patterns.

Employment in the sector remains well below pre-pandemic levels. By 2025, retail employment was 14.4 percent lower than in 2019, the third-lowest recovery among private industry sectors (ahead of manufacturing and construction), even as the City’s total private sector surpassed its pre-pandemic peak in 2023. Retail job losses have been concentrated in industries such as furniture, electronics, and general merchandise stores, while clothing-related retailers and food and beverage stores have added jobs in recent years. Manhattan’s retail workforce has struggled the most, reflecting continued softness in office-dependent foot traffic and tourism that has not fully recovered.

Business trends mirror these challenges. The number of retail firms declined steadily before the pandemic and remains below 2019 levels. Although property values continue to recover more slowly than other commercial categories, the City’s latest property assessment roll does show retail property values recently exceeded the pre-pandemic fiscal year (FY) 2021 level in FY 2027. The average asking rent of vacant retail space has increased every year since the trough in 2021 as retail vacancies and asking rents returned close to pre-pandemic rates in 2025.

Retail workers face additional pressures that existed prior to the pandemic. The sector continues to have one of the lowest-average salaries, a high share of part-time jobs, and a workforce that is disproportionately young, foreign-born and lacking a bachelor’s degree. These characteristics highlight the importance of stabilizing the sector, especially given its role as an entry point for youth and immigrant workers.

Looking ahead, growth is expected to remain uneven. According to the Federal Reserve, increases in spending have been concentrated among higher-income consumers as small retailers reported sharp declines in activity. A likely driver of spending in 2026 will be tourism, as the City expects the number of visitors to continue to approach pre-pandemic levels. However, weaker consumer sentiment, rising energy prices due to the conflict in the Middle East and slower citywide job growth may constrain demand. The sector’s future will depend on how retailers adapt to shifting consumer behavior, inflationary pressures, and a commercial landscape reshaped by hybrid work.

Key Findings

• In 2025, e-commerce continued to reshape the sector, accounting for 16.4 percent of all U.S. retail sales — more than double its share from 2015.

• Retail taxable sales in the City in 2025-26 were 23.3 percent higher than the pre-pandemic 2019-20 level, though it lagged the 34.7 percent increase in total taxable sales, which was driven by sales of services. 
• In 2025-26, the retail sector accounted for 27.8 percent of the City’s taxable sales, the highest share among all major sectors, yet inflation-adjusted retail sales remained 0.9 percent below pre-pandemic levels while total taxable sales increased by 8.3 percent during the same period. 

• In 2025, retail employment was 14.4 percent (49,588 jobs) below 2019 levels, even as total private sector employment exceeded its 2019 level by 4 percent.

• From 2020 to 2025, retail employment increased by only 3.7 percent, the third-weakest recovery among major sectors, behind only manufacturing and construction, which had declines. 
• From 2022 to 2025, only two retail industries, clothing, clothing accessories, shoe, and jewelry retailers (6.8 percent) and food and beverage retailers (4.5 percent) added jobs, while the furniture, home furnishings, electronics, and appliance retailers had the most job losses and the largest employment decline (4,348 jobs; 18 percent) among the retail industries. General merchandise and health and personal care retailers were the next two largest contributors to retail’s job losses (2,862 and 2,457 jobs, respectively). 
• Manhattan’s retail sector fared the worst of the boroughs as retail employment remains 21.2 percent below its 2019 level; Brooklyn has performed the best, but is still 6.3 percent below its 2019 level. 
• Among the 55 Census-defined neighborhoods in the City in 2025, retail employment in only six neighborhoods exceeded their pre-pandemic 2019 levels. Four were in Brooklyn (Bedford-Stuyvesant, Williamsburg/Greenpoint, Crown Heights North and Sunset Park/Windsor Terrace) while two were in the Bronx (Riverdale/Kingsbridge/Marble Hill and Fordham/Bedford Park/Norwood). 

• Retail vacancy rates fell to 5.8 percent in Q4 2025 from the pandemic peak of 6.5 percent in Q1 2021 but is still above the pre-pandemic level of 5.2 percent from Q4 2019.

• Average retail salaries in the retail sector remain among the lowest of all sectors, with the 2025 average of $59,420 well below the City’s total private sector average, even when the high-paying securities industry is excluded ($106,872), and was the second-lowest among all sectors, behind only social assistance. 
• Over 42 percent of retail workers were foreign-born, a much higher share than the nation’s retail share (14 percent) and a slightly higher share than that of all citywide workers (41 percent). 

#### The Pandemic Accelerated Changes in an Evolving

#### Sector

In 2025, retail sales in e-commerce 1 reached $1.23 trillion nationwide, 16.4 percent of all retail sales, up from 7.1 percent from 2015 (see Figure 1). 2 Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the retail trade sector was changing amid the rise of e-commerce. From 2015 to 2019, e-commerce sales increased by 69.5 percent, almost five times the growth of total retail sales (14.4 percent). As a result, by 2019, e-commerce accounted for 10.6 percent of the nation’s retail sales.

The onset of the pandemic forced consumers and retailers to rely even more on e-commerce. From 2019 to 2025, sales in e-commerce more than doubled (120 percent), almost three times faster than total retail sales (41.7 percent). E-commerce has become so ubiquitous that in the latest (2022) reclassification of industries, the U.S. Census removed the electronic shopping industry and the data is now distributed into the rest of the retail industries. As a result, since

2022, there is no available data on electronic shopping.

Even with e-commerce, the pandemic hit New York State (data unavailable for the City) spending especially hard. According to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, New York State’s consumer

spending on goods was flat in 2020, the first year of no growth since 2009. At the same time, the nation’s consumer spending on goods increased by 3.9 percent, a rate even higher than the year before (2.7 percent). Over time, the State has risen more quickly after a sluggish rebound. By

2024 (latest data available), the State’s spending on goods increased by 2.6 percent over the previous year, faster than the increase in the nation’s spending (2.4 percent).

#### Spending Has Recovered but Growth Has Slowed

One way to study trends in local consumer spending is to review taxable sales data. The sales and purchases subject to state and local sales tax include most tangible goods as well as many services, ranging from maintenance services, admissions to places of amusement, restaurant food and drink, professional services, and utility services. Total taxable sales (from all sectors) in

New York City declined by 23.2 percent ($42.4 billion) to $140.2 billion from sales tax year (March through February) 2019-20 to sales tax year 2020-21 because of the pandemic. 3 In the five years since, taxable sales increased by 75.4 percent to reach $245.8 billion in sales tax year

2025-26, 34.7 percent higher than the pre-pandemic 2019-20 level.

Retail taxable sales (sales of goods from only retail establishments) fared better in 2020-21 than total taxable sales as retail sales declined by 11.9 percent ($6.6 billion) to $48.8 billion,

accounting for 34.8 percent of total taxable sales (see Figure 2). Retail sales were not hit as hard, because while the pandemic severely limited consumers from spending on services outside the home, consumers were less constrained to spend on goods because of e-commerce. As a result, taxable sales from electronic shopping increased by 55.4 percent and accounted for over a fifth (20.6 percent) of retail taxable sales, almost double the share (11.7 percent) from the previous year (see the Office of the State Comptroller’s report on NYC Taxable Sales and Purchases).

While retail taxable sales more than recovered the following year, it has had slower growth than total taxable sales in each of the five years since 2020-21, as growth in total sales were led by service industries (i.e., leisure and hospitality, transportation and warehousing, and business

3.8 percent in each of those two years (see Figure 3). In 2025-2026, growth in retail sales rebounded to 3.4 percent, though this still lagged total growth of 5.8 percent. As a result, compared to the pre-pandemic 2019-20 level, retail sales in 2025-26 were 23.3 percent higher, reaching $68.4 billion, while total sales were 34.7 percent higher, reaching $245.8 billion.

The slow growth in retail taxable sales had started even before the pandemic. From 2014-15 to 2018-19, the growth in retail taxable sales lagged behind that of the City’s total every year. As a result, after accounting for a third of total taxable sales in 2014-15, the retail sector accounted for 30.2 percent in 2018-19. The share jumped to 34.8 percent in 2020-21 because of the pandemic, but has since fallen to 27.8 percent in 2025-26, though this is still the highest share out of all major sectors. Because of the reclassification of industries mentioned earlier, it is difficult to determine which industry within retail is holding back growth, though e-commerce is likely still the main driver of growth within the sector.

Growth of taxable sales in the retail sector has lagged behind those of more service-oriented sectors, especially since the pandemic. The three sectors with the next largest shares all had larger increases in taxable sales than retail trade from 2019-20 to 2025-26.
